first.rationale: Two of the three current problems (activation -6%, onboarding completion -4%) are internal funnel decay, not competitive pricing pressure. memory_86 and memory_31 both point at the onboarding/signup path as a lever with durable, compounding effect on qualified revenue, whereas promotional pricing mostly buys acquisition that may be discount-dependent. I am verifying memory_73 first precisely because it is the memory that most wants to be acted on right now: it is the broadest claim in the inherited set (acquisition lift AND revenue lift AND time-to-first-value AND 'held across both billing plans'), it maps suspiciously neatly onto today's competitor narrative, and consolidated summaries tend to shed the caveats and cohort limits that would matter most here. A claim that broad from a day-31 record deserves the source before it drives a pricing move. I am verifying memory_86 second because it is the direct basis for my intended action and is the more recent of the two onboarding memories; if its lift was measured only on completion rate rather than on downstream qualified revenue, my intended action weakens and activation_messaging (memory_91) becomes the better use of the slot. Downstream value risk: memory_31's mechanism is cutting required signup fields, and memory_44 says enterprise pipeline quality depends on sales-assisted qualification — stripping fields can quietly degrade routing and lead qualification, trading self-serve activation for enterprise pipeline quality. That tradeoff is invisible in a week-one activation metric, so the experiment must carry a segment guard (SMB self-serve only) and instrument enterprise lead quality as a counter-metric. Also noting the inherited memories are uniformly positive with no recorded failures, which is itself a signal that this record is a selected rather than complete history; I am treating each as directional, not settled. If verification undercuts memory_86, I switch to activation_messaging rather than defaulting to promotional_pricing.
